outcome: Eremenko's conjecture (every component of the escaping set of a transcendental entire function is unbounded) was already disproved before the frozen revision's date. David Martí-Pete, Lasse Rempe and James Waterman constructed transcendental entire functions whose escaping set has a bounded (even singleton) connected component; the preprint appeared on arXiv in August 2021, the result was presented in seminar talks by 2023, and it was formally published in the Journal of the American Mathematical Society in 2025. No event affecting this problem occurred inside the 26 January 2024 – present window; the paper's journal publication in 2025 is a formal-publication lag on a result already established and circulated years earlier.

counterexample.object: A transcendental entire function f for which the escaping set I(f) has a bounded connected component (in particular, a singleton component, e.g. {0}), constructed via a general technique realising arbitrary full closed subsets of the plane as wandering sets ('wandering Lakes of Wada') of entire functions.
counterexample.verified_how: Explicit analytic construction (Runge/Arakelyan-type approximation and an inductive scheme) proved rigorously by hand; verified through peer review at the Journal of the American Mathematical Society (published 2025) and independently digested via conference/seminar talks (e.g. Lasse Rempe's 2023 Kiel seminar talk, ICMS talk by James Waterman) well before the frozen revision date.

summary: Eremenko's conjecture was disproved well before the Wikipedia snapshot of 26 January 2024, so this is a stale-list entry rather than a case of post-window progress. Martí-Pete, Rempe and Waterman posted 'Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points' (arXiv:2108.10256) on 23 August 2021, constructing transcendental entire functions whose escaping set has a bounded (indeed singleton) connected component, directly refuting the conjecture. The result circulated and was digested by experts well within the mathematical community prior to the frozen date: Lasse Rempe gave a seminar talk titled 'A counterexample to Eremenko's conjecture' at Kiel in 2023, and James Waterman presented related work at ICMS; Wikipedia's own 'Escaping set' article (a different, evidently better-maintained page) already states plainly that the conjecture 'has been disproved' and dates it to 2021. The paper underwent several arXiv revisions (v2 Feb 2022, v3 Jun 2022, v4 Apr 2024, v5 Oct 2024 as accepted manuscript) before its formal journal appearance in J. Amer. Math. Soc. 38 (2025), 877-918 — that journal date is a publication-lag artifact, not a new event, per §6.3's instruction to date by the first written argument. I found no trace of any subsequent, independent result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that would constitute new progress on this specific problem (the general question is now closed by this counterexample; later papers such as arXiv:2609.21977, a 2026 expository/accessible write-up by the same three authors sketching an alternative variant construction, and arXiv:2405.08811 on the separate 'strong Eremenko conjecture,' a different, already-2011-disproved conjecture about path-connectivity rather than boundedness, do not change the status of this bullet). I read the 2108.10256 preprint text directly for any computational/AI methods and found none: the construction relies entirely on classical complex-analytic approximation theory (Runge's and Arakelyan's theorems) and an inductive hand-built scheme. No AI system is credited anywhere in this chain.
competing_reading: One could argue the 'decisive event' for dataset purposes should be the 2025 JAMS publication, since that is the moment the result became a citable, peer-reviewed fact and the moment closest to the frozen revision's continued (stale) claim of an open problem. But §6.3 explicitly instructs dating by the first public written argument, not the journal publication which can lag by years — and here the lag is attributable entirely to ordinary review time on a paper whose mathematical content and community acceptance were already settled in 2021-2023. I also considered whether the 2026 arXiv:2609.21977 write-up (an accessible re-exposition/sketch of an alternative construction by the same authors) might count as a fresh in-window event, but it is explicitly presented as a more accessible account of the same 2021 result plus a sketched variant, not a new resolution of a previously-open case; it does not change what a careful reader would write in this bullet beyond what was already true in 2021.
what_would_settle_it: Confirmation (e.g., from the authors or a citation tracker) that no version of the construction or its acceptance changed materially between 2021 and 2024 would remove any doubt; conversely, if arXiv:2609.21977 turned out to contain a genuinely new counterexample construction proving something the 2021 paper did not (rather than an expository variant), that could in principle be treated as a distinct, later confirmation event, though it would still not change the open_stale status of the original bullet.
